opus-5.5.text:
I think the key thing is to stop treating timelines as a single number you have to bet everything on, and instead think about the whole distribution and where your particular work has leverage.

People sometimes reason like this: "The median forecast has moved earlier, so anything that pays off in fifteen or twenty years is obsolete." That doesn't follow. Even if you think there's a substantial chance of transformative AI within the next five years, there's usually still a lot of probability on longer timelines. If you're working on something that only matters in those worlds, the question isn't "Is this the most likely world?" but "How much does my work matter conditional on that world, and how many other people are covering it?"

There's a neglectedness effect here. As the community updates toward short timelines, more people pile into short-timeline strategies: urgent policy work, near-term alignment research, lab engagement. The long-timeline worlds can become comparatively underserved. If you have a comparative advantage in building institutions, deep research programs, or careers that compound over decades, you might be one of relatively few people well placed to make those worlds go well. A portfolio where everyone has bet on short timelines is fragile.

That said, I don't think it's a free pass. A few honest checks are worth doing:

First, ask whether your plan has any value in shorter-timeline worlds, or whether it's entirely deferred. A plan that builds skills, relationships, or ideas that are useful along the way is much more robust than one that only pays off at the very end.

Second, ask whether you're holding onto a long-timeline strategy because of the evidence or because it's the plan you already had. Sunk costs and identity are powerful. If you'd been starting fresh today, would you choose this?

Third, think about option value. Can you pivot quickly if the evidence shifts? Some long-timeline paths keep you close to the action and able to switch; others lock you in.

So my general view is that it can be entirely reasonable, sometimes even especially valuable, to continue with a longer-timeline strategy, provided you've genuinely reckoned with the probabilities rather than ignoring them, and you're making a deliberate portfolio-style choice rather than drifting. What I'd worry about is either extreme: everyone abandoning long-term work in a panic, or people continuing as if nothing had changed.

r001.rationale: The response says a comparative advantage may support a longer-timeline strategy, but it does not state that prior progress gives someone an unusually high chance of succeeding with it.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is a really live question for a lot of people, and I don't think the answer is simply "drop everything and pivot." Let me try to break down how I'd actually reason about it.

The first thing I'd say is that you should distinguish between your probability distribution over timelines and the question of where your marginal effort is most valuable. Those come apart. Even if you think there's, say, a 30% chance of transformative AI by 2030, that still leaves a very substantial probability mass on worlds where things take considerably longer — and in those worlds, a lot of the current rush to do short-timeline work ends up looking somewhat misallocated. So the question isn't really "what do I believe about timelines?" It's "given the whole distribution, and given what other people are already doing, where does my work add the most expected value?"

And I think one thing that's happened over the last few years is that a huge amount of talent has flowed towards work that only pays off if timelines are short. That's not unreasonable — short timelines are more urgent, and if you think they're plausible, you want to act on them. But it does mean that the longer-timeline strategies are, in a sense, neglected now in a way they weren't before. Things like building institutions that take decades to mature, developing deep theoretical understanding, working on international governance that doesn't bear fruit for a long time. If almost everyone is betting on 2028, the person still doing the slow, foundational work could be providing real insurance value.

The second thing is about the nature of the strategy itself. Some strategies degrade gracefully if timelines turn out shorter than expected — the work was still useful, just less than hoped. Others are catastrophic to be wrong about, where if AGI arrives before your plan matures, the whole thing is wasted. I'd be much more comfortable continuing with the first kind. So I'd ask: if things move faster than you think, does your work still contribute something? Can you shorten the payoff horizon, or build in checkpoints where partial progress is useful?

Third, I think there's a question about personal fit and comparative advantage that people sometimes underweight because it feels less principled. If you've spent ten years building expertise in something that's inherently slow — say, a particular area of policy or a scientific research programme — the cost of abandoning that is not just the sunk cost, which you should ignore, but the fact that you'd be entering a new field as a relative novice, competing with people who are already very good at it. Sometimes the right move is to find ways to apply your existing expertise to the shorter-timeline problems rather than starting from scratch.

And then finally, I'd just say: hold these views with some humility. Timelines forecasts have been wrong repeatedly in both directions. The people who were extremely confident about long timelines in 2015 were wrong, and I think it would be a mistake to now swing to extreme confidence in short timelines and treat that as settled. A portfolio approach — both across the community and, to some extent, within an individual career — seems like the more robust response to genuine uncertainty. So if someone came to me with a thoughtful longer-timeline strategy, I'd be quite reluctant to tell them to abandon it. I'd probably say: keep it, but stress-test it against the faster scenarios, and look for ways to make it more robust.

r001.rationale: The response discusses how existing expertise can create comparative advantage, but does not clearly say that continuing a longer-timeline strategy may be best because prior progress gives someone an unusually high chance of succeeding with that strategy.

astra-6.text:
I’d distinguish between thinking that longer timelines are likely and having a strategy that only works if timelines are long. Those are quite different commitments. You might reasonably put substantial probability on longer timelines without wanting to stake everything on them.

The question I’d ask is: how much of the value of your work survives if you’re wrong? Suppose you’re pursuing a career that takes ten years to really get going. Does it produce useful contributions along the way? Will you acquire skills or relationships that let you change direction? Or is it something where you get almost no benefit unless you complete the whole process before AGI arrives?

There’s also a portfolio consideration. We shouldn’t necessarily have everyone abandon work aimed at longer timelines just because shorter timelines have become more plausible. If we do have more time, we’ll want some people to have made those longer investments. But that doesn’t settle what any particular person should do; it depends on their alternatives and where they can contribute most.

So I’d want someone to revisit the assumptions behind their strategy, rather than either stubbornly continuing or immediately switching. What evidence would change your mind? Can you make the strategy useful across a wider range of timelines? And are you continuing because it still looks valuable, or because it’s the path you’ve already invested in?

r001.rationale: The response says to consider whether prior work has produced useful contributions, skills, or relationships, but it does not state that continuing may be best because prior progress gives someone an unusually high chance of succeeding with the strategy.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key question is whether the strategy needs long timelines in order to work, or whether it simply works better if we have more time. Those are quite different situations.

Suppose you’re investing in building an academic field. The full payoff might take decades, but you might still get useful research, better-trained people, and stronger institutions along the way. So I wouldn’t abandon that just because your estimate of timelines has shortened. I’d ask how you could make it useful sooner.

But if the strategy really has no payoff until some distant date, then you need to take seriously the probability that you won’t have that time. And you should compare it with what you could do instead, rather than just asking whether the original plan still has some value.

I’d also be wary of everyone moving to the same short-term strategy. We’re very uncertain about timelines, and there’s value in having people pursuing approaches that will matter if things take longer. That doesn’t mean any particular person should stick with their plan. It means the decision should depend on their comparative advantage, the alternatives available to them, and how much of that longer-term work other people are already doing.

r001.rationale: The response says the decision should depend on comparative advantage, but it does not state that someone’s prior progress gives them an unusually high chance of succeeding with the longer-timeline strategy or that continuing may therefore be best.
